meta.title: Who really said "Leave it as it is. You can not improve on it. The ages have been at work on it, and man can only mar it"? | Quotle.info

meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Leave it as it is. You can not improve on it. The ages have been at work on it, and man can only mar it'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine. Roosevelt's Grand Canyon speech of 6 May 1903, printed on page 370 of the 1905 collected Presidential Addresses and State Papers.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Roosevelt said it at the Grand Canyon on 6 May 1903, and this exact wording is the one printed in the official text of the address in Presidential Addresses and State Papers, Part One (P. F. Collier & Son, New York, 1905), page 370. The reporter’s transcript of the speech as delivered carries the same thought in slightly different words — the second sentence there reads “Man cannot improve on it; not a bit.”

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: The Works of Theodore Roosevelt: Presidential Addresses and State Papers, Part One
Address at Grand Canyon, Arizona, 6 May 1903
P. F. Collier & Son, New York, 1905 — page 370
The Coconino Sun (Flagstaff), 9 May 1903, p. 1 — “Man cannot improve on it; not a bit.”

source.excerpt: I hope you will not have a building of any kind, not a summer cottage, a hotel, or anything else, to mar the wonderful grandeur, the sublimity, the great loneliness and beauty of the canyon. Leave it as it is. You can not improve on it. The ages have been at work on it, and man can only mar it. What you can do is to keep it for your children, your children’s children, and for all who come after you, as one of the great sights which every American if he can travel at all should see.
trail: The address is printed in full in The Works of Theodore Roosevelt: Presidential Addresses and State Papers, Part One ↗ (P. F. Collier & Son, New York, 1905). The scanned text carries the sentence on page 370, inside a paragraph asking Arizonans not to build on the canyon rim.

A page comparing the two surviving texts sets the Coconino Sun transcript against the official version ↗, and cites the Collier volume by name for the second. The as-delivered version reads “Man cannot improve on it; not a bit.”
Dickinson State University’s Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ carries the full sentence and dates it 6 May 1903 at the Grand Canyon.
The American Presidency Project ↗ files the same remarks under 6 May 1903, Grand Canyon, Arizona.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About Theodore Roosevelt
author.metaLine: 1858–1919 · 26th President of the United States · conservationist
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt (born 27 October 1858, died 6 January 1919) was the 26th President of the United States, serving from 1901 to 1909. He was also a rancher, soldier, naturalist and prolific author, and conservation was the cause he pressed hardest from office. He proclaimed the Grand Canyon National Monument on 11 January 1908, five years after standing in Arizona and asking a crowd to leave the canyon alone.

misattribution.heading: The wording, and the myths around it
misattribution.intro: This one is real — unusually so for a Roosevelt quotation. But the sentence you see quoted is the written version, and a good deal of folklore has grown up around the moment it was spoken.

items.why: The reporter’s transcript, published three days after the speech, has Roosevelt saying “Leave it as it is. Man cannot improve on it; not a bit. The ages have been at work on it and man can only mar it.” The familiar “You can not improve on it” is the official text. As one comparison of the two versions notes, Roosevelt ad-libbed liberally elsewhere, yet this passage is virtually identical between the two ↗.

The 1905 Collier printing sets it as two words, “can not.” Modern reproductions often close it up — the American Presidency Project ↗ prints “cannot.” The meaning is untouched, but the printed source has the two-word form.

The sentence is usually cut here. Roosevelt kept going: “What you can do is to keep it for your children, your children’s children, and for all who come after you, as one of the great sights which every American if he can travel at all should see.” The Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ prints the full passage.

items.who: Roosevelt on a mule, Bright Angel Trail
items.why: The Kolb Studio image almost always paired with this quote is dated 1911 ↗ — a later visit, not the 1903 trip that produced the speech. In 1903 he was at the canyon for roughly eight and a half hours and spoke from a hotel balcony to a crowd the newspaper put at about eight hundred.

items.who: “Roosevelt made the Grand Canyon a national park”
items.why: He proclaimed it a national monument on 11 January 1908. The Grand Canyon National Park Act ↗ was signed by Woodrow Wilson on 26 February 1919, after Roosevelt’s death on 6 January that year.

misattribution.truthLine: The quotation is authentic and precisely dated: Roosevelt, at the Grand Canyon, 6 May 1903, printed on page 370 of Presidential Addresses and State Papers, Part One ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Roosevelt spent about eight and a half hours at the Grand Canyon on 6 May 1903 — part of a long western tour — and used a short speech to make an unusually blunt request of the people who lived there: do not build on the rim. The Santa Fe railroad had just decided against putting its hotel on the canyon’s edge, and he seized on that as the example to follow.

The line has become the shorthand for American preservation thinking, but its logic is worth noticing. Roosevelt does not argue that the canyon is useful, or profitable, or improvable. He argues that it is already finished — that time did the work, and that the only thing human hands can add is damage.
context.detailsSummary: What happened to the canyon afterwards
detailsBody: Roosevelt proclaimed the Grand Canyon a national monument on 11 January 1908, using the Antiquities Act. Full national park status came later: the Grand Canyon National Park Act was signed by President Woodrow Wilson on 26 February 1919, after Roosevelt’s death on 6 January of that year.

The irony was immediate. In the same issue of The Coconino Sun that carried the speech, a short item announced a new hotel to be built at the head of the Grand Canyon Mine Trail, and noted that the Santa Fe would go ahead with its own hotel because travel to the canyon had increased sharply.
